section.title: God Is Our Refuge and Strength
section.sectionRationale: A song of Zion's security amid cosmic and political upheaval, this psalm's opening confession, 'God is our refuge and strength,' and its recurring refrain, 'the Lord of Hosts is with us,' proclaim the very truth fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel, God with us.
section.thesis: Though the earth shakes and nations rage, God's own presence with His people, pictured as a river gladdening the city of God, is unshakable refuge and strength, calling every anxious heart to be still and know that He is God, a peace fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel.
section.frameNote: Three movements marked by Selah: God our refuge amid cosmic upheaval, verses 1-3; God's presence in the city as the nations rage, verses 4-7; and the call to see God's works and be still, knowing He is God, verses 8-11.

units.label: God is our refuge and strength
units.note: God our refuge amid cosmic upheaval

verses.text: God is our {{machaseh|refuge}} and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.
Therefore we will not fear, though the earth is transformed and the mountains are toppled into the depths of the seas,
though their waters roar and foam and the mountains quake in the surge. Selah

units.label: The Lord of Hosts is with us
units.note: God's presence in the city as the nations rage

verses.text: There is a river whose streams delight the city of God, the holy place where the Most High dwells.
God is within her; she will not be moved. God will help her when morning dawns.
Nations rage, kingdoms crumble; the earth melts when He lifts His voice.
The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah

units.label: Be still and know that I am God
units.note: the call to see God's works and be still

verses.text: Come, see the works of the LORD, who brings devastation upon the earth.

He makes wars to cease throughout the earth; He breaks the bow and shatters the spear; 
He burns the shields in the fire.

"Be {{raphah|still}} and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, 
I will be exalted over the earth."
The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah

machaseh.gloss: Refuge, shelter, a place of safety from storm or danger. The psalm opens by naming God Himself, not any earthly fortress, as this refuge, ever present, not distant, in times of trouble.

raphah.gloss: To slacken, let go, cease striving. God's command 'be still' is not mere quiet but a call to release human effort and striving, to stop fighting and trust the LORD's own sovereign action over the nations.

basic.context: Sung by the sons of Korah, this psalm confesses God as refuge and strength even when the natural world seems to collapse, mountains toppling into the sea, and when the political world rages, nations warring and kingdoms crumbling. Its refrain, 'the LORD of Hosts is with us,' anchors confidence not in Zion's walls but in God's own presence.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm does not promise the absence of trouble, mountains genuinely shake and nations genuinely rage, but promises God's unshakeable presence within that trouble, culminating in His own command to cease striving and know that He is God.
basic.originalLanguages: God Himself is called machaseh, refuge, verse 1, not a distant helper but an ever-present shelter. His climactic command in verse 10 is raphah, be still, literally to let go or slacken one's grip, a call to cease human striving and trust God's sovereign action.
basic.typology: The refrain 'the LORD of Hosts is with us,' God with us, anticipates Christ, Immanuel, God with us, Matthew 1:23, while the river gladdening the city of God anticipates the river of the water of life flowing from God's throne in the new creation, Revelation 22:1-2.
basic.christ: The psalm's confidence that God is with His people culminates in Christ, whose very name Immanuel means God with us, Matthew 1:23, and who Himself commands wind and waves to 'be still,' Mark 4:39, the same divine authority this psalm attributes to God alone.
basic.god: God is shown as refuge, strength, and unshakeable presence, active even in apparent chaos, He who both permits the roaring waters and commands the raging nations to be still, ultimately promising to be exalted over all the earth.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 1:23 names Jesus Immanuel, God with us, the fulfillment of this psalm's central confession. Mark 4:35-41 shows Jesus commanding the storm to be still with the same divine authority this psalm ascribes to God. Revelation 22:1-2 pictures the river of life flowing from God's throne, echoing this psalm's river.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's confidence that God's presence is unshakeable refuge amid every upheaval, natural or political, finds its fulfillment in Christ, Immanuel, God with us, who commands the very storms this psalm describes and who will one day be exalted over all the earth in full and final peace.

context.literary:
The psalm falls into three stanzas of roughly equal weight, verses 1 to 3, 4 to 7 and 8 to 11, and each stanza closes with Selah. Twice the same two lines sound like a bell, at verses 7 and 11: the LORD of Hosts is with us, the God of Jacob is our fortress. Many readers think a third copy of that refrain once stood after verse 3, which would have given the song a perfect symmetry, but the psalm as we have it lets the refrain arrive only when the ground has stopped moving.

The stanzas do not describe three different dangers so much as one danger seen from three angles. In the first, the danger is cosmic: earth, mountains and sea. In the second it is political: nations and kingdoms. In the third it is placed in God's own hands, and He is the one who acts. There is also a quiet play on verbs. The nations 'rage' in verse 6 with the same verb used for the waters that 'roar' in verse 3, so the political storm and the sea are the same restless power. The kingdoms 'crumble' in verse 6 with the verb that describes mountains shaking in verse 2 and that the city refuses in verse 5, 'she will not be moved.' Everything around Zion totters, and Zion, with God in her midst, does not.

The last stanza turns from description to invitation and then to a speech. The singer says 'Come, see,' and then God Himself breaks in with the only direct divine words in the psalm, verse 10. The climax is therefore not a pledge from the worshiper but a command from God. The heading names the sons of Korah and 'according to Alamoth,' a direction the footnote treats as probably a musical or liturgical term, compare 1 Chronicles 15:20.
context.historical:
The psalm belongs to the family of Zion songs, together with Psalms 48, 76, 84, 87 and 122, all of which celebrate Jerusalem as the place where God has made Himself known. The sons of Korah were Levitical singers and doorkeepers, so the psalm was sung by people who spent their working lives on the temple hill.

Most readers place the psalm's background in a great deliverance of Jerusalem, and the best known candidate is the Assyrian siege in the days of Hezekiah, when Sennacherib's army stood before the city and was struck down in one night, 2 Kings 19:35-36. The psalm does not name the event, and that silence is useful, because the song could then be sung again in every later crisis. Psalm 76 sings of the same deliverance in similar words: 'There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war,' Psalms 76:3.

The river of verse 4 is a surprise, because Jerusalem sits on a ridge without a river. It has the spring of Gihon and the pool of Siloam, waters that Isaiah calls 'the gently flowing waters of Shiloah,' and he sets them against the roaring flood of the Euphrates, which stands for Assyria, Isaiah 8:6-8. Great ancient cities such as Nineveh and Babylon lived beside mighty rivers. Zion had only a quiet stream, and the psalm says that is enough because the stream is the presence of God. The imagery also reaches back to Eden, where a river went out to water the garden, Genesis 2:10.

To the first singers the language of mountains toppling into the sea would have sounded like the undoing of creation itself, for in the ancient world the sea stood for chaos, and the mountains were the pillars that held the world still. To say God is a refuge even then was to say there is no power in heaven or earth that can outweigh Him.
context.canonical:
Psalm 46 is the first of a small cluster in which the LORD is confessed as King in and over His city. Psalm 47 follows it with a call to all peoples, and Psalm 48 walks around Zion counting her towers. Read together they move from God's presence, to God's rule, to God's city.

The 'God with us' of the refrain is a thread that runs through the Bible. The word 'with us' is the root of Immanuel, and Isaiah, speaking to a frightened king in the shadow of the same Assyrian threat, uses it twice: the child will be called Immanuel, Isaiah 7:14, and to the plotting nations he says 'Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen. For God is with us,' Isaiah 8:10. Matthew hears the same words in the birth of Jesus, Matthew 1:22-23.

The raging nations of verse 6 take us to Psalm 2, which asks 'Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?' and answers that God has installed His King on Zion, Psalms 2:1-6. The promise that wars will cease in verse 9 is the same hope Isaiah sees in the last days, when swords are beaten into plowshares, Isaiah 2:4.

The writer to the Hebrews takes up the shaking language. God once shook the earth, and He will shake both earth and heaven, so that what cannot be shaken remains, Hebrews 12:26-28. Christians are told they are 'receiving an unshakable kingdom,' and the right response is gratitude and worship. Finally the river returns in the last chapter of the Bible, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1-2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wants the people of God to learn where to stand when everything moves. The first step is honesty, because he lists the worst that could happen and does not pretend it will not. Mountains fall into the sea. Nations roar. The point is not that the danger is small but that God is greater, so that 'therefore we will not fear' in verse 2 is a conclusion drawn from verse 1 and not a mood of optimism.

Second, the writer wants the singers to look at God's presence as the real fortress. The city stands not because of its walls but because 'God is within her,' verse 5. The same idea recurs in the refrain, where the fortress is not a wall but a person, the God of Jacob. Jacob was a man who knew flight, fear and wrestling, and to call God his God is to say that this fortress shelters the weak and the guilty.

Third, verse 10 asks something of the hearers. In a psalm full of action, God's word is 'be still.' The first hearers had to choose between hurrying to arm and negotiate, or waiting for God to act. The psalm asks them to do the harder thing: to stop clutching at their own rescue, to remember what God has done, and to let Him be exalted. A worshiper who has sung this psalm has been taught to treat panic as a form of unbelief.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a confession and the experiences behind it. It records what God did for Jerusalem and what the people said about it, and it does not promise that every city, or every believer, will be spared every calamity. Jerusalem herself later fell, and the prophets had to warn the people not to treat the temple as a charm, Jeremiah 7:4. So the psalm cannot be read as a guarantee of safety for any building, nation or institution.

What it prescribes is a stance, and that stance carries over. Believers are to run to God as refuge before they run anywhere else, to sing the refrain out loud when they are afraid, and to obey verse 10 by ceasing to strive. The stillness in view is not passivity. It is the release of a tight grip on our own plans, because the battle belongs to God. Compare Moses at the sea, 'The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still,' Exodus 14:14, and the prophet to Jehoshaphat, 'the battle does not belong to you, but to God,' 2 Chronicles 20:15.

debates.question: Does verse 9, 'He makes wars to cease throughout the earth,' describe a past historical deliverance or point forward to a final, complete peace?

views.label: The verse primarily celebrates God's past historical deliverances of Jerusalem from specific military threats, such as the failed Assyrian siege
views.case: The immediately surrounding verses describe concrete acts, breaking bows, shattering spears, burning shields, language fitting a specific historical battle's aftermath rather than a purely future scene.

views.label: The verse points forward typologically to the final, complete cessation of war in God's eschatological kingdom, as in Isaiah 2:4
views.case: The psalm's climax in verse 10 promises God will be exalted 'among the nations' and 'over the earth' in language exceeding any single historical deliverance, suggesting a trajectory toward final, universal peace.

debates.bearing: Both readings work together: the God who acted decisively in past deliverances is the same God pledged to bring final and complete peace, so the psalm's confidence in present trouble draws directly on the assurance of ultimate future rest.

debates.question: Who is addressed in 'Be still and know that I am God,' verse 10?

views.label: The raging nations
views.case: The verse ends with God saying He will be exalted 'among the nations' and 'over the earth,' and it follows the description of God breaking bow and spear. On this reading God is telling the aggressors to drop their weapons and admit who He is, the natural sequel to verses 6 and 9. The tone would be a warning: stop fighting and recognise the one you are fighting against.

views.label: God's own people
views.case: The psalm's speakers are worshipers who have just been told to 'Come, see the works of the LORD,' verse 8, and the refrain that follows turns back to 'us.' Read this way, the command is a pastoral one to the anxious. It fits the pattern of Exodus 14:14 and Isaiah 30:15, where quietness and confidence are the strength of God's people, and it is the reading that most Christians have sung.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: Because the verb is a plain imperative with no named audience, the psalm may be addressed on two levels. To the nations it means surrender, and to the faithful it means rest. A psalm sung in the temple courts by Israel with the nations in view would allow both.

debates.bearing: The choice changes the tone but not the doctrine. Whether the word falls on enemies or friends, it says the same thing about God: He alone is God, He will be exalted, and no one needs to save the world by their own effort.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 says God is a 'refuge and strength,' and the noun for refuge, machaseh, is from a root meaning to seek shelter, which the Psalms use again and again of taking cover under God, as in Psalms 91:2. The BSB phrase 'an ever-present help' is literally that God has been 'found' to be a help exceedingly, or to the utmost. The verb 'found' carries the sense of proven by experience. Believers have gone to Him in trouble and He has been there. The word for 'trouble' is tsarah, from a root meaning narrowness, so the sense is 'help in tight places.'

Verse 2 begins with 'Therefore,' and the verb behind 'transformed' is the ordinary verb for change or exchange. The earth 'changes,' meaning it gives way, and the mountains slip 'into the heart of the seas,' as the Hebrew has it, a picture of total collapse. The psalm then keeps using the verb mot, 'to totter.' The mountains are shaken, the kingdoms totter in verse 6, and Zion 'will not be moved' in verse 5. The singer chooses one word to say that every other thing may totter and that this one will not.

Verse 4 speaks of streams that 'delight' the city, and the verb is the ordinary one for gladdening. The name 'the holy place where the Most High dwells' uses 'Most High,' elyon, the title of God as ruler above every power, and the verb for 'dwells' is related to the noun mishkan, the tabernacle. In verse 5 'God is within her' is literally 'God is in her midst,' the same preposition that describes God moving among His people in the wilderness. 'When morning dawns' is literally 'at the turning of the morning.' Morning in the Psalms is the time when God acts, and here the help arrives at first light after a long night.

The refrain says 'the LORD of Hosts,' Yahweh tsevaot, meaning He commands the armies of heaven and earth. The word for 'with us,' immanu, is the very form found inside the name Immanuel, Isaiah 7:14. The word for 'fortress,' misgav, comes from a root meaning to be set on high, so it is a place too high to be reached, a lofty refuge that is not merely walls. The same word is used of God in Psalms 18:2 and 9:9.

In verse 10 the imperative 'Be still' comes from raphah, which means to let go, sink down or hang limp, as tired hands do. It is not the word for silence. It says 'let your hands drop.' The next command, 'know,' comes from yada, which in the Bible means to know by experience and acknowledge, not merely to hold a fact. The Hebrew verb for 'I will be exalted' is a form of ruwm, to be high, and it is used twice, once for the nations and once for the earth, a small drum roll. The world will end up looking up.

typology.type: The city and its river, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: Jerusalem had no great river, yet the psalm sings of streams that gladden the city of God. Ezekiel saw water flowing from under the temple threshold, growing from ankle-deep to a river no one could cross, and bringing life wherever it went, Ezekiel 47:1-9. John sees a river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1-2. Jesus cried out at the feast in Jerusalem that whoever believes in Him would have rivers of living water, John 7:37-38. The correspondence rises from a spring in a hill city to the life of God flowing to the whole earth. The type falls short because the psalm's stream sustained one city, while the river of the Lamb gives life to the nations.

typology.type: God in the midst of His city, verses 5 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The refrain says the LORD of Hosts is with us. God's presence in the midst of Israel began in the tabernacle and then the temple, and each was a promise more than a full arrival. In Jesus the promise becomes flesh: the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and Matthew names Him Immanuel, Matthew 1:23. Jesus promised to be with His people 'always, even to the end of the age,' Matthew 28:20, and the city of the last chapters has no temple because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The type falls short in that the temple could be entered only by priests, while the Son dwells with all who trust Him.

typology.type: The shaking of earth and sea, verses 2 and 3
typology.fulfillment: The picture of collapsing mountains and roaring waters is answered by Jesus in the boat, where He rebuked the wind and sea and said 'Silence! Be still!' and it became perfectly calm, Mark 4:39. The disciples' question, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:41, is the question the psalm has already answered about the LORD. Hebrews applies the shaking to the end of the age, when only the unshakable kingdom remains, Hebrews 12:26-28. The correspondence is real, though the psalm sings about God's power to hold, and the Gospel shows that power standing in a human form in the boat.

God breaks the bow, shatters the spear and burns the shields. Isaiah expands the picture to swords beaten into plowshares when the nations stream to the mountain of the LORD, Isaiah 2:2-4. Jesus is that peace: 'He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one,' Ephesians 2:14, having torn down the wall of hostility through the cross. The escalation is that war is ended first at its root, by reconciling people to God and to each other, and will be ended in fact when Christ reigns, Revelation 11:15. The type is unfinished for now, since the world still has wars, and the church waits.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the refrain. 'The LORD of Hosts is with us' is the promise of a presence, and Matthew tells us that the presence has a name and a face: 'they will call Him Immanuel' (which means, 'God with us'), Matthew 1:23. The psalm does not say God will send help from a distance. It says God is in her midst. That is what makes the gospel more than a rescue mission, because in Jesus the LORD of Hosts Himself walks into the trouble. Isaiah's setting is also the psalm's setting, a frightened city under the shadow of Assyria, Isaiah 7:14 and 8:8-10, and the child in that prophecy is a sign that God is not far off.

It leads to Christ by His authority over the sea. The psalm confesses that the waters roar and the mountains quake and yet God is a refuge. In the boat on Galilee, Jesus stands up and speaks to the same forces, and the wind and sea obey, Mark 4:39-41. It is not that the psalm is about the storm on Galilee, but that the disciples' astonished question, 'Who is this?' is exactly the question that Psalm 46 has trained Israel to answer. Only God rules the waves, and here is a man doing it.

It leads to Christ by the stillness of trust. In the garden the psalm's posture is enacted by the Son. He does not call armies, and He tells Peter to put away the sword, Matthew 26:52-53, and He goes quietly to the cross because the battle belongs to God. Paul, in turn, can say 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' after pointing to the cross, Romans 8:31-32. The victory that the psalm celebrates in the breaking of bow and spear is won by the Lamb who was slain.

It leads to Christ by the exaltation in verse 10. God promises that He will be exalted among the nations and over the earth. The New Testament sees that exaltation in Jesus, to whom God gave the name above every name so that every knee should bow, Philippians 2:9-11. The caution is that Psalm 46 speaks first of the God of Jacob and His city, and the New Testament links are drawn from its own language, especially Immanuel, and from Jesus' own works. Not every detail of the psalm, such as the specific river or the ships, is a code for Christ. What it provides is the confession that God is with us, and Christ is where that confession is proved.
study.god:
The psalm gives a rich picture of God as the one who is at once near and high. He is 'ever-present' in trouble, and He is 'the Most High,' verse 4. In many religions the divine is either near and small or high and far. Here the title 'LORD of Hosts' stands next to 'the God of Jacob,' so the commander of the armies of heaven is also the God of a scarred, stubborn patriarch. His power comes with a covenant attached. The refrain joins them: He is with us and He is our fortress.

He is Lord over creation. The psalm imagines the worst that nature can do and puts God over all of it. The seas roar and He does not answer with worry. In the Old Testament, the roaring sea is a picture of the forces that threaten order, and the psalmist places God above them, as Psalms 93:3-4 also does. This does not mean that God causes every disaster, and the psalm does not say who or what shakes the mountains. It only says that whatever it is, it cannot reach past Him.

He is Lord over the nations. The kingdoms 'crumble' when He 'lifts His voice,' verse 6, and the earth melts. The contrast is deliberate: the raging of the nations is a loud noise, and the voice of God is a single sound that ends it. Verses 8 and 9 speak of God who 'brings devastation upon the earth' and also 'makes wars to cease.' The same hand does both. Some readers stumble at this, but the psalm holds justice and peace together: the God who ends the war is the God who judged what caused it, and the desolation is of weapons and pride, not of the meek.

He is the God who acts and the God who asks for trust. The command 'Come, see the works of the LORD' invites observation, since God has left evidence. The command 'Be still and know' invites surrender, since He needs no help. There is a tension here. A believer must 'see' and 'know,' which are active, and also 'be still,' which is passive. The psalm holds them together: we actively rest.

For worship, the psalm gives the church a way to sing in fear. It does not ask us to pretend. It gives us a refrain to repeat until the trembling stops. The sons of Korah, who had once known the anger of God in their own story, Numbers 16, sang that God is a fortress. It is a psalm for people who have a reason to be afraid and a better reason to be quiet.

crossReferences.note: The angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp in a single night, and Sennacherib withdraws to Nineveh. This is the deliverance most often linked with the psalm, in which enemies gather round Zion and are undone without a wall being breached.

Isaiah tells the peoples to gather and prepare, and promises they will be shattered, 'For God is with us.' This is the prophetic parallel to the refrain, with the same Hebrew phrase behind it, and it is spoken in the very crisis when Judah was tempted to trust alliances.

The gently flowing waters of Shiloah are set against the flooding Euphrates. It helps explain the psalm's odd river: Zion's quiet stream is the better water because it is the presence of God, while the flood stands for the empire that seems unstoppable.

Moses tells Israel at the Red Sea to stand firm because the LORD will fight for them and they need only be still. It is the earliest form of the stillness in verse 10, and it links the psalm to the founding rescue of Israel.

Jehoshaphat's people face a vast army, and the prophet says the battle is God's, so they should take their positions and watch. Here the stillness is not idleness but trust that stands ready and lets God be the one who wins.

A sister Zion psalm describing the same kind of victory: flaming arrows, shield and sword are shattered, and horse and rider lie stunned at God's rebuke. Reading it with Psalm 46 shows the shared memory of deliverance behind both.

The nations rage and the kings plot against the LORD and His Anointed, and God laughs from heaven, then installs His King on Zion. It shows the same conflict as Psalm 46:6 from the side of God's throne, and it points to the Messiah as the answer to the raging.

In the last days the nations stream to the mountain of the LORD and beat their swords into plowshares. This is the fulfilment of the promise of verse 9 that wars will end, and it explains why the psalm can speak of God's peace as certain.
Jesus rebukes the wind and sea, and they obey. The disciples ask who this is. The psalm's confession that God is a refuge when the waters roar meets a man who speaks to them and they settle.

God shakes earth and heaven so that only what cannot be shaken remains, and believers receive an unshakable kingdom. It takes the psalm's language of things that totter and gives it an end: the church stands where the earth's mountains do not.
If God is for us, who can be against us? Paul answers the psalm's question of fear with the cross: God did not spare His own Son. The confidence of the refrain now has a price paid in full behind it.

The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side. It is the final form of the psalm's river, and the city it gladdens is the whole new creation.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question that runs from Genesis onward: what is stronger than chaos? At creation God spoke over the deep and the waters were held in their place, Genesis 1:2 and 1:9. The flood showed what happens when the waters are released, Genesis 7:11. The psalm takes that ancient fear of the sea, and of the mountains falling, and says that even if the deep returned God would still be a refuge. It is a song that trusts the Creator to be bigger than un-creation.

It also answers a question about the nations. From Babel onward the peoples gather against God or apart from Him, Genesis 11:1-9, and in the Psalms they rage, Psalms 2:1. In Israel's history, Egypt, Assyria and Babylon each played the part of the roaring sea. The psalm's answer is that God's presence in the midst of His people is the one fixed point. The sanctuary is not a shelter because of its stones, and the prophets who came later insisted on that, Jeremiah 7:4. When the temple was burned, the psalm did not fail; it sent the faithful looking for a better city.

That search finds its centre in Christ. God comes to be with us in the flesh, and the storm is stilled by His word. He goes into the shaking of the cross and the dark, and bears the blows that the world's rage could deliver. His people are told they belong to an unshakable kingdom, Hebrews 12:28, and that the God who is for them did not spare His Son, Romans 8:32.

The story ends in the new creation, where the sea is no more, Revelation 21:1, and the river of life flows without threat. The city is no longer defended, since its gates are never shut, Revelation 21:25. The nations who once raged now walk by its light and bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:24. The stillness of verse 10 becomes the rest of those who have nothing left to fear, because God dwells with them, Revelation 21:3.

sermon.title: Trusting God in Difficult Times, Psalm 46
sermon.why: In this meditation from his special series for difficult times, Keller works through Psalm 46 to show how naming God as refuge and strength, and hearing His command to be still, meets present fear and upheaval with settled confidence in God's presence.

quiz.q: What image portrays overwhelming trouble in verses 2-3?

options.text: Mountains toppling into the sea and roaring, foaming waters.
options.note: The psalm uses cosmic upheaval, the collapse of mountains and sea, as its picture of the worst possible trouble.

options.text: A gentle breeze disturbing calm waters.
options.note: The imagery is of violent, overwhelming upheaval, not a gentle disturbance.

options.text: A drought drying up the land.
options.note: The psalm's imagery is of overwhelming water and shaking mountains, not drought.

options.text: An army approaching from a distance.
options.note: Verses 2-3 use cosmic, natural imagery; armies and nations appear later, in verse 6.

quiz.q: What is present in the city of God, according to verse 4?

options.text: A river whose streams delight the city.
options.note: The river symbolizes God's own gladdening, life-giving presence within His city.

options.text: A towering fortress wall built by human hands.
options.note: The text names a river, not a human-built wall, as the source of gladness.

options.text: A great army stationed permanently at the gates.
options.note: The psalm's confidence rests in God's presence, symbolized by the river, not in military garrisons.

options.text: A marketplace filled with foreign traders.
options.note: The verse specifically names a river gladdening the city, not commercial activity.

quiz.q: What command does God give in verse 10?

options.text: "Be still and know that I am God."
options.note: This command calls people to cease striving and trust God's sovereign action over the nations and the earth.

options.text: "Take up arms and fight for your own defense."
options.note: The command is the opposite, to cease striving and let God act, not to take up arms.

options.text: "Flee to the mountains for safety."
options.note: The command calls for stillness and trust, not flight, in the face of danger.

options.text: "Build higher walls around the city."
options.note: The psalm's confidence rests in God's presence, not in human fortifications, and the command is to be still, not to build.

quiz.q: What title is repeated as a refrain in verses 7 and 11?

options.text: "The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress."
options.note: This refrain anchors the psalm's confidence in God's abiding presence and protection.

options.text: "The mountains will never be moved."
options.note: The psalm actually says the mountains can be toppled; the refrain is about God's presence with His people, not the mountains' stability.

options.text: "Our own strength will never fail."
options.note: The refrain credits God, not human strength, as the source of security.

options.text: "The nations will never rage again."
options.note: The psalm acknowledges the nations do rage, verse 6; the refrain's confidence is in God's presence despite that raging.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's confidence connect most directly to the New Testament?

options.text: Christ is Immanuel, God with us, the fulfillment of this psalm's central confession of God's presence.
options.note: Matthew 1:23 names Jesus Immanuel, directly fulfilling this psalm's refrain that God is with His people.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The psalm's language of God's presence and stilling power is directly picked up in the Gospels, especially Matthew 1:23 and Mark 4.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of Christ's return.
options.note: The psalm speaks of God's presence and coming exaltation, not a specific date for any future event.

options.text: It is fulfilled only in the physical rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.
options.note: The psalm's deepest fulfillment is in God's presence with His people in Christ, not merely in physical construction.

questions: The psalm names God as refuge and strength even while mountains topple and waters roar. What upheaval in your own life right now makes it hardest to believe God is truly your refuge?
God's presence, not Zion's walls, is what makes the city unshakeable, verses 4-5. Where are you tempted to trust in your own defenses rather than in God's presence with you?

God commands, 'Be still and know that I am God,' in the middle of raging nations and crumbling kingdoms. What would it look like this week to actually stop striving in a specific situation and trust God's sovereign action instead?

This psalm's refrain, 'the LORD of Hosts is with us,' is fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel, God with us. How does remembering that Jesus Himself is God with you change how you face today's specific troubles?
The psalm ends with God's promise to be exalted among the nations and over the earth. How does hoping in that final, universal peace shape how you respond to present conflict or fear?

translationNotes.note: Refuge renders machaseh, a place of shelter from storm or danger, here applied directly to God Himself rather than to any physical fortress.
The city of God identifies Jerusalem or Zion, though no literal river of this scale ran through the city, pointing beyond the literal terrain to God's own life-giving presence.
Be still renders raphah, to slacken or let go, a command to cease human striving and effort rather than merely to be quiet, addressed as much to warring nations as to anxious hearts.
